extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling a novel's point of view and the relation between pictorial narration and dramatic scene-making; how to authenticate the narrator, when to use first person, and how to economize dramatic enactment. Focused on novel-length fiction technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticate the point of view / dramatize the seeing eye
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mind that knows the story and the eye that sees it remain unaccountable, the novel shows an unsatisfactory want of finish; the only way to silence questioning of the narrator’s authority is to make the mind and the eye objective—i.e., to make them facts in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the narrator's point of view within the book (so it can be recognized and verified there) rather than leaving it as an unexplained omniscient presence. Examples/explanations: an unaccounted-for omniscient voice leaves the book with an 'inconclusive look' or a 'loose end'; dramatizing the recorder gives the whole book equal finish. (See Thackeray's early omniscience contrasted with later works that 'pack up the loose end'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a conspicuous omniscient author unless compensated
rubrics_metrics.description: An omniscient author who is conspicuous may be a defect: it can create thinness in the general impression and make parts of the book seem less authoritative unless the author’s personal force (genius or charm) overpowers the defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with conspicuous authorial intrusion—while charm or genius can make it acceptable, otherwise it will feel like an arbitrary, unmeasurable factor that diminishes the novel’s authority on rereading. Turgenev and Thackeray are used as contrasting examples of authorial presence and its effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the narrator (make the narrator a visible, dramatic fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to authenticate a reported impression is to make the recorder/narrator himself a piece of action—'a play within a play'—so that the reader perceives the narrator’s position and line of sight as part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in-character first-person narration or otherwise bring the narrator among the characters so the reader sees who the seer is and where he stands (Esmond vs Vanity Fair). Benefits include measurable line of sight, sharper relief for characters (Beatrix example), and a tone that is part of the story rather than arbitrary authorial manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between pictorial method (broad vista) and dramatic enactment (intensity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pictorial method (broad, travelling glance over many facts) allows coverage of large spaces and quantities of experience; dramatic enactment (scenic presentation) supplies intensity and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the trade-off and use both where appropriate: rely on pictorial narration for breadth but shift into enacted scenes where intensity and a heightened impression are required (as plot thickens or climax approaches). Novelist’s skill shows in guiding story into and out of scenes, making narration do dramatic work when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economize dramatic scenes—reserve drama for important occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is the novelist’s highest light and should be used sparingly and with purpose; overuse lessens its force where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoard dramatic enactment for occasions that demand emphasis (e.g., climaxes) rather than using it constantly in quotidian moments. The economical procedure is to 'hoard' drama so its power is not wasted (Bovary used as example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend authorial vision with character consciousness to avoid intrusive intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: When the author’s vision is blended subtly with a character’s perception, the author's intervention becomes unobtrusive and the point of view feels governed by the character rather than imposed from without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate Flaubert’s technique of mingling his acuter vision with Emma’s, so that the character’s vision seems to govern the story and the narrator’s voice is less insistently felt—this strengthens the picture without exposing an external, unverifiable authorial mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid untestable, purely authorial pronouncements
rubrics_metrics.description: Information or judgments that 'openly come straight from' the author and cannot be tested by the reader reduce the picture’s authority and weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, anchor judgments in scenes, character perception, or verifiable detail rather than relying on narrator-as-observer to pour undemonstrated information into the reader's ear (Turgenev criticized for this tendency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat recollection as dramatic action when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of calling up recollections can itself be rendered as a piece of action so that the reflexive mind becomes an immediately perceptible dramatic fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the narrator’s recalling process visible—show the effort, placement, and effect of memory—so that the framed vision is authenticated by an observable recorder rather than being a disembodied report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first person when it provides necessary unity, precision, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration in character substitutes a known 'I' for the general authorial 'I', giving a delimited field of vision, precision, individuality, and a tone that is part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer first person when the design benefits from a defined vantage point (e.g., long retrospects like David Copperfield or adventures like Harry Richmond). It supplies a comfortable assurance of point of view and personal colour that situates the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of using first-person autobiography to disguise formlessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Autobiographical first-person narration 'composes of its own accord' and its natural waywardness can be used to excuse or hide formlessness in a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the charm of autobiography to cover structural weaknesses; formlessness may be mistaken for valid artistic form when presented as memoir, so ensure underlying design justifies the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overtax first person when the subject demands dramatization of inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: When the hero is the subject of the book (a portrait requiring the representation of inner growth and moral/emotional history), expecting the first-person narrator merely to report will be insufficient; the subject’s consciousness needs dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novel’s central aim is to portray a character’s inner development (Meredith’s Harry Richmond), consider dramatizing moments of inner change rather than relying solely on retrospective reporting by the protagonist, since the latter may fail to give the necessary 'substance' of the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply dramatic techniques to pictorial passages to retain advantages of both methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Method can be imposed upon method: dramatize aspects of the pictorial chronicle so as to strengthen it toward the power of drama while keeping its breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze where pictorial narration is weakest (narrator authority, lack of intensity) and use dramatizing devices—in-character narration, enacted recollection, scenes within retrospection—to correct the weakness without sacrificing the panoramic scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft scenes with care—avoid neglect and waste of scenic possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: In many quotidian novels the possibilities of the scene are abused: scenes are either neglected in treatment or recur too often and are wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give scenes proper treatment when they occur; do not overuse them trivially or treat them perfunctorily. A scene should be composed and used to its full dramatic effect when it appears, otherwise reserve such moments for truly consequential episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let point-of-view choice determine tone and the weight of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of narrator affects the tone and the convincing weight of comments: when we know who sees (Esmond) the tone has meaning within the story; when the author stands in a void (Thackeray) the manner trails away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious that first-person/in-character narration embeds the narrator’s tone as part of the story (giving it authority), while a detached omniscient voice risks sounding merely authorial manner. Use POV to give assertions and reflections a referent within the story.
